cutting.intro: Trim lightly to keep Ficus elastica tidy and healthy.
bullets: Every 2–4 weeks, remove yellow, spent, torn, or damaged leaves and any soft, unhealthy tips.
Shorten leggy stems just above a leaf node to encourage fuller growth and better shape.
Use clean, sharp pruners and wipe blades before cutting to reduce sap spread and disease risk.

support.intro: Support is only occasionally needed for Ficus elastica indoors.
bullets: Check stakes or ties every 4–8 weeks for tightness and stem rubbing.
Make sure any stake stays firm, and guide new upright growth loosely if it starts leaning.

aeration.intro: Light aeration helps if the soil surface starts to compact.
bullets: Every 2–3 months, gently loosen the top 2–3 cm (0.8–1.2 in) with a stick or small fork.
Aerate sooner if water sits on the surface or the top layer feels hard and dense.

cleaning.intro: Clean the plant every 2–4 weeks to keep foliage working well.
bullets: Wipe leaves gently with a soft damp cloth, supporting each leaf underneath to avoid tearing or bending.
Remove fallen debris and rinse the saucer and pot exterior to reduce dust, improve appearance, and limit pest hiding spots.

humidity.intro: Extra humidity is usually only occasionally needed for Ficus elastica indoors.
bullets: Check weekly in dry rooms and use a pebble tray or humidifier if leaf edges brown or crisp.
If misting, do it lightly 1–2 times weekly and keep leaves dry overnight to limit spotting.

mulching.intro: Top-dressing is optional but useful for indoor Ficus elastica.
bullets: Refresh a thin 1–2 cm (0.5–0.8 in) layer of bark fines or coco chips every 3–6 months.
It helps slow surface drying and buffers soil temperature without keeping the mix soggy.

watering.intro: Water the India Rubber Tree on a simple repeat schedule.
bullets: Every 7 days is a useful guide, but wait until the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry or leaves start to droop slightly.
Soak the soil evenly until excess drains out, then empty the saucer so roots do not sit in water.
Avoid small frequent sips, which keep the surface damp and can encourage root problems.

fertilize.intro: Feed the India Rubber Tree lightly during active growth.
bullets: Apply a balanced houseplant fertilizer at 1/2 strength every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer.
Add fertilizer to already moist soil, then water lightly so nutrients spread through the root zone.
Pause feeding in fall and winter, and avoid overfeeding, which can cause salt buildup and leaf stress.

repotting.intro: Check regularly and repot only when the root ball is crowded.
bullets: Inspect every 6–12 months for roots at drainage holes, slowed growth, or water running straight through the mix.
Move up 2–5 cm (1–2 in) wider into a pot with drainage, not an oversized container.
Use a fresh, well-draining chunky mix to support steady moisture without waterlogging.
Lift and turn leaves to check undersides, examine the stem base, and look into drainage holes for roots or trapped moisture.
If roots circle tightly, pests appear, or the base feels soft, plan follow-up care such as repotting, isolation, or watering changes.

monitoring.intro: Do a quick visual check every 5–7 days.
bullets: Look at leaf color and texture, new growth, soil moisture, and overall posture for early signs of stress.
Scan for pests while checking the leaf surfaces and stems, then adjust light, watering, or placement if anything looks off.

careDetails.aboutPlant:
Ficus elastica, commonly called India rubber tree, is a broadleaf evergreen grown as a houseplant and, in warm climates, as a large tropical tree. It is known for thick, glossy leaves and an upright, woody growth habit.

This species is native to eastern South and Southeast Asia. Indoors it is usually straightforward to grow, but size, sensitivity to sudden changes, and irritating sap can make care for India Rubber Tree slightly less beginner-proof than smaller foliage plants.

It does best with bright, indirect light, slightly moist but well-draining soil, and moderate humidity.

careAdvice.title: Rotate for Balance
careAdvice.description: Turn the pot 90° every 1–2 weeks during active growth to keep the canopy even and reduce leaning toward the window, which is especially useful when growing India Rubber Tree indoors.

careAdvice.title: Clean Leaf Surfaces
careAdvice.description: Wipe the leaves with a damp soft cloth every 2–4 weeks to remove dust, improve light capture, and make early spider mite or scale infestations easier to spot.

careAdvice.title: Stake Tall Stems
careAdvice.description: Use a slim stake and soft ties if the main stem starts to lean, especially in larger indoor specimens, so new growth stays upright without stem damage.

careAdvice.title: Check Sap Safety
careAdvice.description: Wear gloves when pruning, repotting, or taking cuttings because the milky sap can irritate skin, and keep pruned material away from children and pets.

careAdvice.title: Watch for Edema
careAdvice.description: If small corky spots appear on leaves, reduce watering frequency slightly and improve air movement, as this often signals roots are taking up water faster than the leaves can use it when caring for India Rubber Tree.

soil.intro: Ficus elastica needs an airy, moisture-retentive mix that drains quickly.
bullets: Use a loamy, organic-rich base with chunky structure rather than dense, fine-textured compost alone.
Blend houseplant mix with pine bark and perlite; optional coarse sand can further improve drainage and root aeration.
Aim for slightly acidic to neutral soil, about pH 6.0–7.0.
Avoid heavy garden soil or mixes that stay soggy, compact easily, or trap water around roots.

water.intro: Water when the upper soil layer has partly dried.
bullets: Check the top 2–3 cm (1 in) and water only when it feels dry, then soak thoroughly and let excess drain away.
Ficus elastica usually needs more water in spring and summer and less in autumn and winter as growth slows.
Yellowing leaves, soft stems, or sour soil suggest overwatering; drooping, curling, or crisp leaf edges suggest the root zone stayed too dry.

soilPH.intro: Slightly acidic to neutral soil helps Ficus elastica absorb nutrients well.
bullets: Aim for pH 6.0–7.0 in a well-draining mix.
Test with a soil meter or kit. Lower pH with sulfur, raise it with lime.
Wrong pH can cause nutrient lock-out, pale new leaves, and chlorosis.

pruning.intro: Pruning helps Ficus elastica stay tidy and well shaped indoors.
bullets: Trim in spring or early summer when growth resumes most strongly.
Remove dead, damaged, or crowded stems and any yellowing leaves.
Cut just above a node to encourage branching and a fuller shape.
Use clean, sharp pruners and wear gloves because the sap irritates skin.

humidity.intro: India rubber tree prefers 40–60% humidity and usually manages average indoor air.
bullets: It tolerates somewhat dry air but may show brown edges or curling when air stays very dry.
Low humidity can also cause slower unfurling and crispy leaf margins, especially near heaters.
Raise humidity with a pebble tray, grouped plants, or a humidifier while keeping airflow steady.

sunlight.intro: Ficus elastica grows best in bright, filtered light for steady leaf growth.
bullets: Provide 6–8 hours of bright indirect light or 2–4 hours of gentle morning sun daily.
India Rubber Tree tolerates partial shade, but lower light often causes slower growth, longer gaps between leaves, and smaller foliage.
Avoid strong afternoon sun, especially in summer, because direct exposure can scorch leaves; move brighter in winter if light drops.

container.intro: This species grows well in containers when drainage and stability are managed carefully.
bullets: Use a pot with drainage holes and empty any collected runoff promptly so roots do not sit in water.
Choose a container only 2–5 cm (1–2 in) wider than the root ball to limit excess wet soil around roots.
A heavier terracotta or ceramic pot helps counter the top-heavy canopy and reduces tipping as Ficus elastica grows.

placement.intro: Place this plant in bright indoor light or a warm, sheltered outdoor position.
bullets: India Rubber Tree grows best indoors near an east- or south-facing window with filtered sun.
Allow 30–60 cm (12–24 in) of space for airflow and even growth.
Avoid cold drafts, heating vents, and harsh direct midday sun that can scorch leaves.

fertilizer.intro: Ficus elastica benefits from light feeding during active growth.
bullets: Use a balanced houseplant fertilizer, compost, or a slow-release formula.
Feed every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer at 1/2 strength.
Reduce to little or no feeding in fall and winter as growth slows.
India Rubber Tree can suffer from salt buildup, so avoid strong doses.

winterCare.intro: Winter care matters because this tropical plant is not frost tolerant.
bullets: Keep it above 18°C (64°F) and away from cold drafts or glass.
Move container plants indoors before nights drop below 13°C (55°F).
Do not mulch indoor pots; instead insulate roots by keeping them off cold floors.
Reduce watering slightly and keep bright, indirect light on the foliage.

propagation.intro: Propagation is commonly done from cuttings or by seed, though cuttings are preferred.
bullets: Take stem cuttings in spring or summer from healthy, firm growth.
Let cut ends dry briefly, then root in moist mix with bright, indirect light.
Keep warmth near 21–27°C (70–81°F) and moderate humidity during rooting.
Seeds need warmth, steady moisture, and patience, but are less common indoors.

temperature.intro: Warm, stable conditions support the best growth and leaf quality.
bullets: Aim for 65–81°F (18–27°C) for active growth, with the steadiest results around 68–77°F (20–25°C).
Avoid long exposure below 55°F (13°C); growth slows in cool weather, and cold drafts can mark or drop leaves.
Frost can damage or kill this plant, while heat above 90°F (32°C) is tolerated better if light is filtered and soil moisture stays even.

repottingAndTransplanting.intro: Repotting supports steady growth and prevents root crowding in containers.
bullets: Repot in spring or early summer when roots circle the pot or growth slows.
Most plants need a larger container every 2–3 years.
Move to a pot 2–5 cm (1–2 in) wider with fresh, well-draining mix.
Keep the root ball intact, water after repotting, and avoid harsh sun for 1–2 weeks.

facts.text: This species was once tapped for latex in its native range, which gave rise to names like rubber plant and Indian rubber tree. It was historically important before Hevea brasiliensis became the main commercial source of natural rubber.
facts.title: Rubber source history

facts.text: In tropical conditions, it can begin life as an epiphyte and later send roots downward that thicken around the host tree. This hemiepiphytic habit is shared with some other figs and can eventually overwhelm the support tree.
facts.title: Strangling root habit

facts.text: Like other true figs, it has a highly specialized relationship with fig wasps for pollination. Outside its native ecological range, the plant is usually grown for foliage and rarely produces viable seed without its specific pollinator.
facts.title: Fig wasp pollination

interestingFacts.didYouKnow: Its large, leathery leaves emerge wrapped in a red sheath called a stipule, which protects the new leaf as it expands and then drops away.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Scale insects
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Wipe pests off with a damp cloth or cotton swab, then wash leaves thoroughly. Treat repeat outbreaks with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, covering stems and leaf undersides, and isolate the plant until controlled.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects attach to stems and leaf undersides and feed on sap. Symptoms include sticky residue, yellowing leaves, and gradual loss of vigor.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Spider mites
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Rinse the foliage well, especially the undersides, and raise humidity to 40–60%. Follow with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil every 7–10 days until new damage stops.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These pests are more likely in dry indoor air and can cause fine stippling, dull leaves, and light webbing between leaves and stems. Heavy infestations can lead to leaf drop.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Mealybugs
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove visible insects by hand with a cotton swab dipped in alcohol, then clean the plant carefully. Repeat treatment with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil and check hidden stem nodes weekly.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects gather in leaf joints and along stems, where they appear as white cottony clusters. They weaken growth by feeding on sap and may leave sticky honeydew.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Anthracnose
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Prune off affected leaves with clean tools and keep foliage dry when watering. Improve airflow, avoid crowding near windows, and discard fallen debris so spores do not persist around the plant.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease can cause irregular brown or black lesions on leaves, often starting at edges or damaged tissue. In humid, crowded conditions, affected leaves may yellow and drop early.

faqs.question: Warum werden die Blätter meines Gummibaums gelb?

faqs.answer: Ja. Er wächst gut in Töpfen und wird häufig jahrelang drinnen gehalten. Wählen Sie einen stabilen Topf mit Drainage und rechnen Sie mit regelmäßigen Umtopfungen, wenn die Wurzeln den Platz ausfüllen. Er kann schließlich einen kleinen Topf überwuchern.
faqs.question: Kann der Gummibaum in Töpfen angebaut werden?

faqs.answer: Ja. Der Saft ist giftig für Haustiere und Menschen und kann die Haut reizen. Wenn er gekaut oder geschluckt wird, kann er Mundreizungen, Erbrechen und Durchfall verursachen. Halten Sie ihn von Kindern und Tieren fern und tragen Sie Handschuhe beim Schneiden.
